articles.title: AI-native brokerages bring in nearly $1 million per employee in Zywave report
articles.desc: A new Zywave study finds automated brokerages grow revenue faster than headcount, and clean data may pay off in carrier bonuses too.
articles.content: AI-native brokers near $1M revenue per employee AI-native brokerages bring in nearly $1 million per employee in Zywave report A new Zywave study puts AI-native brokerages at close to $1 million in revenue per employee, versus about $175,000 at traditional agencies. Zywave’s data points to the back office as a key source of the gap, even as producer roles grow. It also argues cleaner, automated data can affect carrier bonus commissions, which run from 0.43% to 6.74% of premium on one published schedule. When a carrier bonus can swing fifteenfold on loss ratio alone, the data work that trims an agency’s back office can also influence the size of its contingent or bonus check—especially if it helps keep the book in better loss-ratio tiers. Revenue per employee is the planning number to track: about $175,000 at traditional agencies and close to $1 million at AI-native brokerages, while P&C headcount grows by less than 1% a year. Survey adoption overstates readiness. Nearly three-quarters of brokerages report some AI use, but only 13% use it across multiple parts of the business. Turn your Business Services expertise into content. Record interviews, organize footage, and write with AI on a free trial of the MarketScale platform for qualifying companies. No demo required, no credit card. A traditional US insurance agency brings in roughly $175,000 for every person on its payroll. An AI-native brokerage brings in close to $1 million, nearly six times as much. Zywave, the Milwaukee-based insurance technology provider, documents that gap in a new study, reports. The figure is not a projection. Economics like these are already splitting the US distribution market in two. The Milwaukee insurance technology provider built the comparison from employment data, commission structures and technology adoption across US distribution. Its main conclusion is milder than the ratio. AI is not taking the broker's seat. Firms that have automated their back offices are growing revenue faster than they add staff, though, and the distance between them and everyone else can already be measured. Picture an agency principal deciding whether to hire the next account manager or buy the next workflow tool. The useful question is which part of the business the gap actually sits in. 's data points to the back office. It also points to a second payoff few agencies connect to automation at all: the carrier bonus check. More than half of agency staff, 55.6% by Zywave's count, still work in service and back-office roles. That means chasing documents, re-keying data and handling routine policy servicing. These are the tasks AI is taking over first, and the change already shows up in the staffing mix. Clerical and data-entry jobs fell from 32.3% to 30.6% of agency employment in the year through May 2025, the steepest decline on record for that category. Producer roles rose to 29.1% over the same period. Taken together, those figures describe agencies moving people into different jobs more than cutting them. The roles that handle paper are shrinking. The roles that face clients are growing. The hiring market leaves little room to do it any other way. A labor pool that can't carry growth on its own Insurance professionals projected to retire between 2021 and the end of 2026, with no equal pipeline behind them Actual P&C industry headcount growth, January 2025 to January 2026 Headcount growth the industry had expected over the same period U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics; Q1 2026 Insurance Labor Market Study by The Jacobson Group and Aon's Strategy and Technology Group For agencies that plan growth around new hires, those numbers change the math. A talent pool growing by less than 1% a year can't staff a book that grows faster than that. That makes revenue per employee the more useful planning figure. articles.title: Plenty of Retirees Tour Margaritaville and Never Buy. The Costs Beyond the Mortgage Are Worth Pricing First
articles.desc: The mortgage ends, but four other bills at a Margaritaville-style community never do, and only one of them has a cap. Learn which documents expose the real monthly number before you sign anything.
articles.content: Plenty of Retirees Tour Margaritaville and Never Buy. The Costs Beyond the Mortgage Are Worth Pricing First - 24/7 Wall St. Plenty of Retirees Tour Margaritaville and Never Buy. The Costs Beyond the Mortgage Are Worth Pricing First Published November 21, 2026, 11:39am ET · 4 min read This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Buyers touring active-adult model homes tend to focus on the mortgage payment. A separate question determines affordability: what living there costs each month, even with the loan paid off. Latitude Margaritaville sells active-adult living to buyers fifty-five and older, and plenty of people take the tour and never buy. The ones who walk away usually back out over the carrying costs nobody put on the whiteboard. Four Bills That Show Up Whether or Not There’s a Mortgage Four things sit next to the mortgage: HOA and club dues, community development district assessments where a CDD exists, property taxes and insurance. Each one is documented in records outside the sales office. The HOA’s declaration and current budget show what the dues cover and how much the reserves hold. Communities like Latitude at Daytona Beach have their own association, and its budget is the document to read. If there’s a CDD, its charges show up on the county tax bill as non-ad valorem assessments, so county property appraiser and tax collector records show the exact line for a comparable home. Insurance quotes, both homeowners and flood, on the specific address show the actual premium, since Florida premiums vary widely by carrier and location. Property taxes have a wrinkle for newcomers. The bigger break is portability. Under § 193.155(8), a buyer who held a Florida homestead exemption in any of the 3 immediately preceding years can carry part of that old assessment advantage to the new house. Someone moving from Ohio has nothing to carry over, so their first bill is based on full just value. What Each Monthly Fee Costs in Portfolio Dollars Every $1,000 a month in carrying costs comes to $12,000 a year. At a 4% withdrawal rate, that takes about $300,000 of portfolio. A buyer retiring at 55 who needs the money to last 35 years or more is often modeled closer to 3.5%, and at that rate the same $1,000 takes about $343,000. That is the portfolio cost of a fee schedule, and it is also why the old 4% rule deserves a second look (we walked through why it wobbles now, and the income-first alternative, in a As a baseline, the average aged couple who both collect Social Security will get $3,355 a month after the 3.6% COLA in 2027, or $ 40,260 a year. Average annual household spending nationally is $81,905. That leaves a gap of $41,645, which takes roughly $1.04 million to fund at 4%. Florida isn’t cheap, either. The BEA puts its price level at 103.414 against a national 100. No state income tax helps, but a month per person, about $5,026 a year for a couple. . Buyers in their late 50s rely on ACA marketplace coverage until they become eligible for Medicare, and subsidy eligibility depends on taxable income. how fast a homestead’s assessed value can rise, but property tax bills can still rise faster when tax rates or assessments increase. HOA dues get reset by the board every year. CDD operating assessments follow the district’s budget. Insurance follows rebuilding costs and the reinsurance market. None of those three are tied to the cap. In the Deltona-Daytona Beach-Ormond Beach metro, the FHFA home price index rose 38.64% over five years but slipped 0.17% in the latest year. The cap keeps a homesteaded tax bill from tracking a run like that. Insurance replacement costs and community operating budgets get no such protection. Over time, the uncapped costs can make up a larger share of what owning the home costs each month, while Social Security rises only with CPI-W. articles.title: Sky Harbour: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
articles.desc: Its fixed-rate debt, with the 2061 bonds locked at 4.18%, insulates the company from credit swings while it builds out its hangar campuses.
articles.content: Sky Harbour: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors | The Motley Fool Sky Harbour entered third-party construction with $38 million in initial contracts. Third-quarter revenue increased 45% year over year to support campus openings. Management raised full-year revenue run-rate guidance to $44 million to $48 million. 10 stocks we like better than Sky Harbour Group › On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, reported a 45% year-over-year increase in revenue while expanding construction activity across its airfield campuses. The company continues to spend heavily on building specialized home-based hangar campuses to capture high-margin rental income as newly constructed facilities stabilize. Three things management said stand out. 1. Sky Harbour Opens Third-Party Construction as a New Revenue Line Management expanded into manufacturing pre-engineered metal buildings and general contracting for external partners to exploit excess capacity at its steel fabrication facility. We are recognized by everybody in the industry as having the best hangar in business aviation... Why do not we start manufacturing and even general contracting for third parties? It is not the secret sauce, but it is a really interesting new revenue line. -- Tal Keinan, CEO and Chair of the Board 2. Capital Allocation Shift Focuses Growth on Top-Tier Airport Locations The business is concentrating its land acquisition and leasing resources on tier 1 premier airports, where revenue per available square foot starts at $50, to maximize yield on invested capital. What I think you can expect to see over time is increasing percentage of our revenue capture per square foot at tier 1 campuses... focus at least in the coming, call it, year or 2 is going to remain on the tier 1 campuses. -- Tal Keinan, CEO and Chair of the Board 3. Fixed-Rate Debt Structures Protect the Business From Rate Increases Management hedged its existing debt obligations and capital lines through long-term fixed rates and swaps, insulating corporate funding costs from broader credit market volatility. All of our debt is fixed rate. Our 2061 bonds are fixed at 4.18% until they mature in 30 years. Our JPMorgan facility is swapped for 4 years to an effective 4.73% even for the amount we have yet to draw. Construction pace is setting corporate records across multiple markets, and leadership accepts near-term operating expense increases to secure long-term campus scale. Operating leverage, in-house steel fabrication, and direct ground-lease negotiations provide structural advantages as leadership tracks pricing discipline and initial lease-up velocity. We expect a marked increase in gross profit and EBITDA margin expansion with these added revenues and limited increases in operating costs given the ability to use the same personnel and equipment with an expanded campus doubling size. Filling 826,000 square feet of hangar space in 2027 remains the leasing team's primary operational hurdle. Pricing power on renewal leases underpins long-term margin goals. Our leases feature annual escalators of CPI with a floor of 4%. And when they expire and the new lease is signed, that same square foot goes at an average of a 20% markup of the already accelerated. -- Tal Keinan, CEO and Chair of the Board When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. articles.title: K-State Salina Selected as an Inaugural NOAA Cooperative Aviation Center
articles.content: K-State Salina Selected as an Inaugural NOAA Cooperative Aviation Center | Area | derbyinformer.com purchase a subscription to continue reading. You have permission to edit this article. KANSAS REFLECTOR SCREEN CAPTURE/U.S. SENATE YOUTUBE CHANNEL WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) – chairman of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, and Science – recently announced that Kansas State University Salina (K-State Salina) has been selected as one of three universities to participate in the inaugural National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Cooperative Aviation Centers (NCAC). Sen. Moran’s legislation, which was signed into law in 2020, created the initial NOAA Aviation Accession Training Program, which later became NCAC. This program aims to establish partnerships with universities to create a pipeline of qualified pilots for the NOAA Corps. “K-State Salina’s selection as one of the first NOAA Cooperative Aviation Centers demonstrates the university’s strong legacy of training the next generation of pilots,” said Sen. Moran. “I worked to establish this program to help address the shortage of qualified NOAA pilots while providing a direct pipeline from our local universities to the NOAA Corps. Pilots studying at K-State Salina will now have the opportunity to receive the training they need for a career with the NOAA Corps, conducting research, weather forecasting and collecting critical data for communities across our state and nation.” “This partnership opens a door for our students to careers they may never have imagined: flying into hurricanes, supporting weather research and gathering data that communities depend on,” said Alysia Starkey, CEO and dean of Kansas State University Salina. "We are grateful to Sen. Moran for his vision in creating this program and for his steadfast support, which has given our students access to the advanced equipment and simulation technology that made this selection possible." In his role as the lead Republican of the subcommittee that funds NOAA, Sen. Moran has consistently secured federal investments for NOAA aviation training, including $5.5 million for K-State Salina to purchase advanced aviation training equipment and a custom full-motion flight simulator. These investments were critical in helping position K-State Salina to be selected as one of NOAA's first three Cooperative Aviation Centers and will continue to support the university's training partnership with NOAA. Student applications will open for the two-year program in August 2027. Selected students are expected to enter the program in fall of 2028, intern at NOAA's Aircraft Operations Center (AOC) during summer break of their junior year and graduate in the summer of 2030. NOAA plans to select up to two students from each university in the program’s first year, with the ability to scale in the future dependent on demand. Students enrolled at or accepted by K-State Salina, Florida Institute of Technology and University of North Dakota are eligible to apply. articles.title: FBI investigating apparent hack of a key criminal justice information database, AP source says
articles.desc: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database
articles.content: FBI probing hack of its national criminal justice database: AP source - WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta FBI investigating apparent hack of its key national criminal justice database, AP source says of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday. The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics. The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.” News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, . There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers. a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau's jobs portal. the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. articles.desc: That Intel or AMD sticker on your PC might not tell the whole story. Find out how Windows can show which GPU you really have and how it is performing.
articles.content: Where you can find which GPU you have in your Windows PC | United States Where you can find which GPU you have in your Windows PC That Intel or AMD sticker on your PC might not tell the whole story. Find out how Windows can show which GPU you really have and how it is performing. In case you didn't know, your Windows computer can house two graphics processors, and the one powering up your display isn't always the one keeping those games running. Some laptops juggle integrated graphics for everyday use and a dedicated NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPU for heavier workloads. An Intel or AMD sticker on your system doesn't always tell you the whole story. Confirming a game's requirements, troubleshooting system performance or deciding if your PC could use an upgrade first needs a proper look at the internals. Thanks toand AI data centers putting pressure on memory supplies, PC builders are already bearing the brunt of it. Ejae and Darlene Love Perform at Macy’s Holiday Windows Unveiling It's best to know how capable your current setup is before you burn a hole in your wallet. The good part is that Windows can easily identify your graphics hardware for you without needing any additional software or taking a screwdriver to your PC. While Task Manager is the fastest way to go about it, there are a couple of other built-in tools you can use when the details are hidden in fine print. Windows' Task Manager can do more than just flag which apps and services are eating up your computer's resources. The Performance section gives you a clear look at the graphics card and spells out the details about its memory, driver and even the current workload it is under. Don't take the numbering of the GPUs at face value. For instance, GPU 0 isn't always assigned to the more powerful graphics card or the one that's running all your games. Windows simply labels the GPUs based on hardware location, and this has nothing to do with their performance.that's available on a dedicated GPU, while shared memory is regular system RAM that the GPU borrows when needed. Some integrated GPUs even have a portion of system RAM reserved for graphics. Windows reports this as dedicated memory, but an integrated GPU mostly relies on the system RAM. Besides the GPU branding, you also get driver details, info about DirectX and even GPU temperature in Task Manager. Your PC's Device Manager is exactly where you need to look for your GPU's name without any graphs involved. To begin, right-click the. You'll find all the graphics devices listed by Windows and also see whether your PC has both integrated and dedicated GPUs. Once you find the GPU you want, double-click on it and open theinstead of your graphics card's name in Device Manager, it means Windows is using a generic display driver. articles.content: Waymo recalls robotaxis after they drove into closed freeway lanes | United States Waymo recalls robotaxis after they drove into closed freeway lanes The recalls come after the California DMV banned Waymo from operating on its state freeways. Waymo filed a pair of recalls for its robotaxi fleet following incidents where its vehicles drove into closed freeway lanes and didn't follow manual commands from emergency responders. As first reported by, the Alphabet-owned company said the two recalls were"to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control. California Bans Waymo Driverless Cars From Freeways After Construction Zone Incidents " Waymo cars will operate normally on city streets, while freeway drives remain on pause as the company works on software improvements to address the issues.from state freeway use. The state's DMV called the robotaxis an"imminent hazard to public safety" following a few incidents where Waymo vehicles drove into construction zones that were closed to traffic. According to the California DMV, three Waymo robotaxis entered restricted construction zones in the city of Burlingame on separate occasions. A Waymo robotaxi was also seen trying to navigate around a California Highway Patrol car that was performing a traffic break. "Yesterday, we filed two voluntary recalls on our automated driving system to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control," a Waymo spokesperson told Engadget. "These are standard steps in our rigorous safety approach to validating and refining our technology as we scale to more complex driving environments. " Waymo said that it's still working on a remedy for the closed freeway lanes recall, but added that there were no collisions or injuries from this issue, according to. articles.title: Whole-Earth simulation could boost search for alien life
articles.desc: This model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets.
articles.content: Whole-Earth simulation could boost search for alien life - Futurity You are free to share this article under the Attribution 4.0 International license. Scientists have built a whole-Earth simulation to help find life on other planets. It’s a dizzyingly busy time for scientists searching for life on distant planets. To date, astronomers have cataloged more than 6,000 planets beyond our solar system and are searching the atmospheres of the most promising worlds for chemicals that might be byproducts of life. Astrobiologists are particularly interested in atmospheres like Earth’s that trap enough heat to support liquid water on the planet’s surface, which scientists consider the key factor in determining whether a planet can support life as we know it. But scientists also want to distinguish between habitable and inhabited worlds. To do that, they need to know what sorts of atmospheric conditions on a planet can be explained without life, so that they can identify planets with atmospheres that can only be explained by life’s influence. To provide that planetary baseline, University of Washington researchers built a complex virtual Earth with one crucial tweak: no life. , the researchers simulated the Earth’s geochemical systems for 5 billion years—from its formation 4.5 billion years ago through roughly 500 million years in the future. The simulation modeled the exchange of chemicals between the core, mantle, crust, surface, and atmosphere over time. It accurately predicted 19 planetary properties like heat flow through the mantle, but left out the influence of life on those systems. The simulation can be generalized to predict how an atmosphere might evolve on any rocky planet, and can help pinpoint evidence of life in atmospheres that don’t fit the model. “This model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,” says lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who completed this research as a UW doctoral student of astronomy and is now a postdoctoral fellow at UC Riverside. “When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.” Gilbert-Janizek’s work builds on a model developed in the lab of senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy. Earlier versions of the model simulated the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation, but did not include the surface or atmosphere. A planet’s atmosphere is shaped by many nonbiological factors, including heat and gases from the interior and from the planet’s star. But the atmosphere of a distant planet is also where astronomers hope to spot explicit evidence of life. There are many ways that life might change an atmosphere: On Earth, plants and animals pump steady streams of oxygen and methane into the sky. Those two elements destroy each other when they mingle. Thus, an alien astronomer studying our planet might suspect that something alive is replenishing the supply of both gases. That logic led human astronomer Gilbert-Janizek to add surface and atmosphere modeling to the existing Earth simulation, completing the picture of how chemicals move through all of the Earth’s systems. The result is a model that can be tuned to study any rocky exoplanet that astrobiologists find interesting. Researchers can plug in basic details about that planet and run the simulation to see whether the model can reproduce the observed atmosphere without the influence of life. If they can’t get a match, the planet in question gets even more interesting. “Dr. Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” Barnes says. “After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface, and atmosphere. articles.title: Fossilized Jaw And Teeth Of Giant Elephant, Believed To Be Of Palaeoloxodon Species Found In MP's Raisen
articles.desc: The fossil has been sent to a lab in Bhopal for preliminary examination by a team of ASI, report Alok Kumar Srivastava and Amit Dubey.
articles.content: Fossilised Jaw And Teeth Of Giant Elephant, Believed To Be Of Palaeoloxodon Species, Found In MP's Raisen Fossilised Jaw And Teeth Of Giant Elephant, Believed To Be Of Palaeoloxodon Species, Found In MP's Raisen The fossil has been sent to a lab in Bhopal for preliminary examination by a team of ASI, report Alok Kumar Srivastava and Amit Dubey. Archaeologists digging the spot where the fossil was found : The fossilised jaw and teeth of a giant elephant were discovered at Patai Ghat on the banks of Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh's Raisen district. The fossil is believed to be that of a prehistoric elephant. Following the discovery on November 10, a team of experts from Bhopal, Lucknow, and Pune arrived in Patai on Saturday. ASI experts excavated the fossil, extracted it, and took it with them to Bhopal for examination. The fossil was securely packed under the supervision of Prof Vijay Sathe of Deccan College University, Pune, and Dr Anjali Trivedi, who had arrived from Lucknow. The fossil will first be sent to a laboratory in Bhopal for preliminary examination. After testing and analysis, experts will decide whether to send it to the Birbal Sahni Institute in Lucknow for detailed scientific investigation or to conduct the research in Pune. The fossil will be jointly studied by the ASI team, along with Dr Trivedi's team and Vijay Sathe, a professor of palaeontology from Pune. The jaw of the elephant found in Patai is approximately 75 centimetres long and 25 centimetres wide. (ETV Bharat) The jaw of the elephant found in Patai is approximately 75 centimetres long and 25 centimetres wide. The jaw bones appear to be arranged in seven to nine rows parallel to each other. The structure features 11 tooth-like projections on one side and seven on the other. The teeth in the fossil are high and prominent. Furthermore, the lower part of the jaw (chin) is broad. According to preliminary information from experts, the fossil may be approximately 4,00,000 to 5,00,000 years old. It may belong to the Palaeoloxodon species, but the exact details will emerge after further investigation. Experts said in prehistoric times, elephants were 4 to 5 metres (approximately 13 to 16 feet) tall and weighed 18 to 22 tons. Dr Trivedi said, "According to preliminary studies, the fossil may be from the Quaternary Period. Elephants found during the period were much larger than modern ones. They stood up to 12 feet tall and weighed several tons. The exact species and other characteristics of the fossil can only be confirmed after a detailed scientific study." She said, "The Archaeological Survey of India is preserving this fossil. The Narmada Valley is a very rich region in terms of fossils. Many dinosaur and elephant fossils have been found here earlier. If the area of ​​the Narmada Valley is studied scientifically, there is a possibility of finding even more important fossils in the future." Prof Sathe said, "The jaw has been safely removed from the soil. It will now undergo detailed testing and chemical analysis. Only then will authentic information regarding the species, age, and other characteristics of the creature be revealed". He added, "For the last several years, we have been researching the evolution of organisms and the environment of the time, from approximately 2.5 million years ago to 12,000 years ago. The fossil found in Patai could prove vital in understanding the ancient natural history of the Narmada Valley." The fossilized teeth of the elephant (ETV Bharat) The team of experts said the fossil was found in a layer of yellow soil. Scientists have studied the soil layers and geological structure of the site where the fossil was found. The layer of yellow soil is geologically considered to belong to the Baneta and Sohagpur Formation. The layer dates back to the Pleistocene period, estimated to be between 24,000 and 5,00,000 years ago. Can buyers hold the old breakout area? Bessent says Trump and Xi saw robust discussion on trade policy, AI University of Michigan consumer sentiment 51.5 versus 51.5 estimate Greer says US-China trade truce extension hinges on rare earths Canada retail sales comes in stronger at 0.8% vs 0.7% estimate. Core up 1.0% vs 0.7% estimate. Morning Kickstart. Anthropic slides after its IPO and gold breaks lower investingLive European news wrap: Stock markets remain under pressure, bonds rally on slowdown expectations North American market wrap | Friday, November 20, 2026 Stocks got hammered into the close. Anthropic gave back much of its first-day gain, and Nvidia’s losses deepened after Reuters reported that the SEC was examining the chipmaker’s accounting practices. The selling spread across the AI trade, from semiconductors to data-center suppliers. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261 points and wiped out its gains for the year. The S&P 500 fell for a seventh straight session. Treasuries and the yen caught a bid, but lower yields did little to slow the selling in stocks. Gold, silver and Bitcoin fell alongside equities. Oil went the other way as renewed U.S.–Iran escalation risk kept traders focused on supply through the Strait of Hormuz. FX. Yen leads, Aussie lags The dollar was mixed, with the dollar index nearly flat at 103.891 late in the session. The USD was weakest against the yen, with USDJPY down 0.71% to 158.54, and strongest against the Australian dollar, with AUDUSD down 0.57% to 0.6618. USDCHF fell 0.43% to 0.8402. The USD gained against the kiwi and edged higher against the Canadian dollar. EURUSD and GBPUSD were both flat. USDJPY covered 142 pips, 156% of its 22-day average daily range. AUDUSD reached 140% of its average and USDCHF reached 116%. EURUSD and GBPUSD covered just 66% and 75% of their averages, respectively. Treasuries. The 10-year is back below 5% 2-year 4.649%, −13.0 basis points 5-year 4.7403%, −12.6 basis points 10-year 4.9438%, −10.8 basis points 30-year 5.3298%, −7.1 basis points The front end led the move lower in yields, steepening the curve. The 2-year fell 13 basis points even after Fed Governor Lisa Cook argued for tighter policy. The bid for Treasuries held as stocks made new lows. images.investinglive.com. Will the Fed save the market or will they fight inflation? Pres Trump wants the Fed to ease policy despite the inflation? The chance of a Fed stands pat in December is close to 9% now. U.S. stocks. A bruising end to the week Dow industrial average 48,147.33, −1.93% Friday, −8.0% for the week. S&P 500 6,910.39, −3.70% Friday, −8.6% for the week. Nasdaq Composite 22,617.73, −5.28% Friday, −10.0% for the week. Russell 2000 2,581.79, −2.76% Friday, −7.5% for the week. Nasdaq 100 −5.6% Friday, −10.4% for the week. AI and chips take the biggest hit Nvidia closed down 13.8%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 10.7%. The selling reached beyond chips. AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell 12.1%, and Bloom Energy dropped 15.3%. Anthropic fell 9.1% to $88.30 in its second session, still above its $83 IPO price. General Mills gained 3.7% as consumer staples found some buyers. investinglive.com Europe. DAX leads the declines German DAX 24,801.22, −2.60% Friday, −7.29% for the week. French CAC 40 7,927.75, −1.89% Friday, −5.27% for the week. UK FTSE 100 10,346.33, −1.02% Friday, −5.10% for the week. Spanish IBEX 35 18,873.09, −1.63% Friday, −5.73% for the week. Italian FTSE MIB 48,703.73, −2.48% Friday, −6.08% for the week. investinglive.com U.S. data and the Fed Final November University of Michigan consumer sentiment rose to 51.5 from 48.0 in October. The bigger move was in one-year inflation expectations, which fell to 3.7% from 4.3% in the preliminary report and 4.7% in October. Five-year expectations eased to 3.3% from 3.5% in October. Cook said September’s rate hike had done too little to curb inflation and warned that waiting could make it harder to bring inflation down. investinglive.com Oil rises as Iran risk returns to focus WTI was up 1.53% at $83.70 late in the session, and Brent was up 0.71% at $92.63. The Financial Times reported that President Trump was weighing renewed strikes on Iran. The risk of disruptions through Hormuz helped support crude even as the equity selloff raised questions about demand. investinglive.com Gold, silver and copper slide Gold fell 2.41% to $3,537.77, silver dropped 3.84% to $41.224 (remember when it surged to $121 at the beginning of the year?), and copper lost 3.01% to $5.4640 and trades lower on the year now. A flat dollar index and falling Treasury yields would ordinarily help gold. Its decline alongside equities is consistent with investors raising cash. The heavier losses in silver and copper also fit with concerns about industrial demand. investinglive.com Bitcoin breaks $60,000 Risk off. Bitcoin was down 4.86% at $58,902 late in the session. It traded with the broader selloff in risk assets, and the break below $60,000 added pressure to Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood. What I’m watching Monday Can chip stocks hold a bounce with the Nasdaq indices closing just above the 100 week MAs, and does the 10-year yield stay below 5%? Those are two quick reads on whether Friday’s selling is easing. Oil remains the market to watch for any weekend developments around Hormuz. The next U.S. growth check comes with Monday’s flash PMIs at 9:45 a.m. ET. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
